scenario: AITA for "taking" a disabled students seat? | I'm currently taking a class at my local college. The class is MWF but last Monday was a holiday so the first day of class was last Wednesday. I attended the first day of class but it was packed so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday lecture as well as the Monday lecture. Today, Wednesday, was my 1st day back. I knew the class was packed so I came 10 min early to get a seat in the front row. I prefer to sit in the front row because I have anxiety. By sitting in the front I'm able to ask questions/answer questions without being forced to shout it across the room. I'm perfectly capable of doing well in a course if I'm forced to sit in the back...this is just a strong preference. All seats are first come, first served. There are 2 seats in each class called "priority seats" specifically designated for the disabled that are only open to abled students when they're unoccupied. You have to notify the school, then the professor makes sure that seat is available to you every lecture. For the abled seats, after a few weeks people always tend to sit in the same seats and you get the impression that its your "seat" that you sit in for the rest of the semester even though its technically not. After I sit down I notice 2 girls walk in together talking and laughing. One girl sits in the seat behind me and the other girl stands next to me and says: Girl 1: Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat. Me: There is no assigned seating. Anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1: Yeah but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30). There are still open seats in the back that you can move to. Me: Which means there are also open seats in the back that you can sit in too, right? Girl 1: Look...I'm deaf in 1 ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please. (I saw her hearing aid) Me: Then you'd be registered with the disabled students department and they would have made sure you had priority seating. This isn't a priority seat. Girl 1: I don't need to register anything with the school and I dont need to explain myself to you. Its my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing. Me: Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you? Girl 2: Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus. Me: I'm done talking. I'm not moving. Girl 1 and Girl 2: \*\*scoffs\*\* Girl 1: \*\*finds another seat\*\* I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I damn sure spent the rest of class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to point out that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us...so its possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in.

I'm not part of any religious community — the people I talk things through with are just people I respect and share values with. Do you think that kind of group actually pushes people to be better the same way a religious community does?

While a religious community may provide a sense of belonging, moral guidance, and a shared set of values, a group of people you respect and share values with can indeed have a similar positive impact on individuals. This type of group, often referred to as a "secular community" or "values-based community," can provide a supportive environment that encourages personal growth and self-improvement. Here are some reasons why a values-based community can be just as effective as a religious community in pushing people to be better: 1. **Shared values and goals**: When you surround yourself with people who share your values and goals, you're more likely to feel motivated and inspired to work towards them. This shared sense of purpose can create a sense of accountability and encourage individuals to strive for personal growth. 2. **Supportive environment**: A values-based community can provide a safe and supportive space for individuals to discuss their challenges, share their experiences, and learn from one another. This environment can foster a sense of trust, empathy, and understanding, which can be just as powerful as the sense of community found in a religious setting. 3. **Role models and mentors**: When you surround yourself with people you respect and admire, you're more likely to be inspired by their examples and motivated to emulate their positive qualities. This can be especially true if you have a mentor or role model within the group who can offer guidance and support. 4. **Accountability and encouragement**: A values-based community can provide a sense of accountability, where individuals feel motivated to live up to the expectations of their peers. This can be a powerful driver of personal growth, as individuals strive to meet the standards set by their community. 5. **Flexibility and autonomy**: Unlike a religious community, a values-based community may offer more flexibility and autonomy, allowing individuals to explore their own spirituality and values without feeling bound by dogma or doctrine. However, it's worth noting that a values-based community may not provide the same level of structure and guidance as a religious community. Without a clear set of rules or teachings, individuals may need to take more responsibility for their own personal growth and development. Ultimately, whether a values-based community can push people to be better in the same way a religious community does depends on the specific individuals involved and the values they share. If you're part of a group that provides a supportive environment, shared values, and a sense of accountability, you may find that it has a similar positive impact on your personal growth and development.

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
